speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) whether the Ministry has implemented safeguards, including longitudinal studies, to monitor the impact of early AI use at the primary level on students’ development of foundational skills and higher-order thinking and to prevent over-reliance on AI tools; and (b) if so, what these entail.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: My response will also address related oral and written Parliamentary Questions scheduled for the Sitting on and after 7 May.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: General purpose AI is also easily available online.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is therefore important for students, even younger ones, to develop overall awareness of AI in daily life, have guided discussions on its benefits and risks, and be ready to use AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: AI is going to cause disruption and create opportunity, and we want to prepare our children well and equip them with the knowledge and skills to meet this new world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are what we call the "Four Learns".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our students also need well-designed and supervised hands-on experiences, through the use of educational AI tools guided by teachers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This spiral approach, as students progress through different levels in school, prepares them to harness AI to benefit their learning, critically evaluate AI output and guard against risks such as cognitive offloading.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We want to develop AI literacy in our students in a calibrated and purposeful way.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our approach is informed by research on how children learn and develop, and what is helpful at each stage of growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Technology, including AI, is used only when it supports educational objectives and students’ development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This has guided us when introducing AI in our schools.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: From Primary 4, our students would have developed foundational literacy, numeracy and basic foundational knowledge of AI in their daily lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Research also shows that at around this age, they would have developed some executive functioning skills – like planning, task initiation and ability to evaluate their own thinking – to begin to use simple digital tools to support their learning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will therefore let them use educational AI tools under teacher supervision.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Students in Primary 4 to 6 will only use AI tools in school that are specifically designed for education.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And they will only do so under teacher supervision.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This includes the AI-enabled tools that we have introduced into the Singapore Student Learning Space (SLS) which are specially designed to help our children and students learn.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, Primary 4 students in an English Language class can use the AI Learning Assistant (LEA) in SLS for composition writing in class.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Using the prompts provided by their teacher, our students can get ideas on how to "show not tell", a technique where students enhance their writing through details on actions and emotions to help readers better experience the narrative, and refine their drafts based on personalised feedback from the LEA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In this case, the LEA supports students to iteratively improve their writing with more engaging content and vivid language, to strengthen their writing skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The LEA gives every student an individual AI writing coach that responds to our students in real-time, based on their specific drafts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As a guardrail, the LEA will redirect students back on track if they veer off-topic and ask irrelevant questions, or if they want to be spoon-fed with direct answers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Last year, my colleagues and I tried it out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We were in a class, there was a particular topic, and we deliberately tried to go off course and say "What is good in the canteen?" or "How can I use this topic for a party trick?" And they will tell us to say "No, this is not relevant.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, our teachers can reinforce our students’ AI literacy during lesson consolidation by guiding them to form good learning habits when using AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As students learn to use AI and learn with AI, they will also learn more about what AI is.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They are taught how it works, how to be discerning about AI output and the importance of being responsible for the content that they create.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: During Cyber Wellness lessons, students are taught to be discerning about AI output as it may contain errors or false information and the importance of being responsible for the content they create.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Prior to using AI tools in SLS, students go through the “Basic Module on AI and AI-enabled Features in SLS”, to teach them about the tools in SLS and how to use them for learning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is a programme which includes coding, computational thinking and introduction to AI, so that students appreciate AI’s benefits, risks and limitations, and understand how AI uses data to learn.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Schools will also teach students when they should not use AI, so that they do not take short cuts to get answers without actual learning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We want to provide our students with a school environment where they can develop good learning habits and understand the importance of upholding academic integrity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, some secondary schools may design tasks which allow students to use AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In these situations, students must state where they have used AI and cite the sources of information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This helps to prepare them for post-secondary education where they will be expected to use AI far more heavily, in anticipation of what their future workplace might look like.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, if students pass off AI-generated content as their own, they will have to bear the consequences of academic dishonesty.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If students use AI as a shortcut for their daily work instead of learning deeply, they will not be able to demonstrate the levels of mastery expected during the exams.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In cases where the use of AI is permitted in national exams, such as for coursework, Teacher Supervisors monitor students’ work such that AI use meets the objectives of the assessment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Educational AI tools made available by MOE have in-built safety guardrails to protect learners’ interest, privacy and well-being.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When schools use commercial-off-the-shelf AI tools, they are required to check that the input data does not contain personal identifiable information and is in compliance with data management guidelines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our teachers play a central role in harnessing AI effectively for student learning, and we have been equipping them with the necessary knowledge and skills to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, we provide opportunities for our teachers to learn about AI, including the ethical and pedagogical considerations of its use, and its associated risks and limitations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also facilitate the sharing of good practices on AI use amongst our educators.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include workshops and networked learning communities led by our Master Teachers as well as online sharing platforms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At MOE, we seek to keep up-to-date with international reports and how other systems are approaching the use of AI in education.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also fund projects that study how AI affects children’s development and learning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But given how quickly AI is developing, we are also working with our schools to conduct short-term research to inform classroom practices in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We know that some parents have misgivings about exposing their children at an early age to AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many are already struggling with their children’s excessive screentime on smart phones and devices at home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through the Parents Gateway and MOE’s social media platforms, we have been sharing with parents how schools use AI and how parents can support their children’s use of AI in their education journey.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some schools even meet parents at the start of the year or at different points in time, to engage them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The recent post titled “We answer: How your primary school child is learning with AI” on MOE social media is one example.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Schools also share with parents how AI tools may be used in teaching and learning at the school level and provide avenues for parents to share their views on the use of AI tools.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: AI has been developing rapidly and is increasingly embedded into everyday systems around us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If we are not mindful, we may lose the consciousness in detecting the presence of, and influence that AI has in our decision making and ways of thinking, simply because it works so seamlessly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, development of AI literacy is critical and must be timely.
Education systems across the world are responding to this differently.
Some systems like China, UAE and the United Kingdom (UK) have introduced AI – AI literacy, AI use – from Primary 1.
Others like India or states in Australia and the United States (US), start at similar ages to Singapore, or slightly later.
MOE has chosen to take a calibrated approach informed by the learning sciences, emerging research and studies conducted by practitioners and academics and ongoing exchanges with various countries.
As AI develops and more research is done, we will continue to calibrate and adjust our approach to the use of AI in education.

Even as we prepare our students to be future ready, I want to assure parents and fellow Singaporeans that the use of AI in education seeks to be balanced and age-appropriate, and applied purposefully to support students' learning and development.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Number one, how do we ensure that our students still learn to think independently, even with the use of AI?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Number two, will the AI curriculum account for the needs of vulnerable students, such as those with special needs and mental health challenges?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And number three, will the Ministry also consider studying the impact of AI on vulnerable children and those from at-risk families as well?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We want to make sure that even as our children start to use AI tools for learning, or use AI tools for their schoolwork as they grow older, that it scaffolds and enhances cognitive development and metacognitive development, and not hobble it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, independent learning, independent ability is an important part of AI in education.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are two broad concepts, the heuristics that guide us and beneath that there are guidelines, principles and quick guides that enable us to adjust and adapt the use of AI in the classroom, as well as on SLS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With regard to students with special educational needs (SEN) and mental health, as I have said yesterday and previously, we have SEN officers in school.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have student school counsellors, we have teachers who are given basic foundational knowledge on how to support students with education needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the classroom as well as, under teacher supervision, the use of AI-enabled tools in SLS will continue to be under teachers' supervision, and for children with SEN, they will keep an eye out for them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We do not use our chatbots or AI tools to check on students' well-being, or to help them build up social emotional skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is the sole domain of our educators and our MOE staff.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we use it on the cognitive front to help our children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When it comes to children from more vulnerable families, if there are specific issues that may impact their use of AI in learning, then our schools will specifically support them and scaffold for them,

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, many parents I have spoken to are worried about cognitive offloading – the phenomenon where children offload their thinking to AI.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Metacognition, the ability to notice when you are wrong, is built through struggle and not through receiving correct answers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And the evidence is that students who encounter difficulty before resolving it, develop stronger self-correction capacity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, how does MOE intend for our learners to encounter productive struggle to build these metacognitive skills?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, Sweden's Karolinska Institute advised the Swedish government, and I quote, "There is clear scientific evidence that digital tools impair rather than enhance student learning", end quote.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I am sure the Minister is aware of this, so what are his points of disagreement with the Swedish example?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And number three, some parents have also asked if they will have the option of opting out their children from specific aspects of AI tool usage in classrooms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: You try the SLS Mathematics question, guided by LEA Mathematics, it will not spoon-feed you the answer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But these are not used in the MOE space in SLS, and it will then remind you to say, "No, this approach is wrong".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some say it is a Socratic style, but it prompts you so that it causes you to go back and revisit the principle you have learnt and it will not spoon-feed you.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Of course, our concern for parents is that the children may use tools outside SLS at home, use general purpose tools to take shortcuts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And that is why the home-school partnership is so important.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The partnership between parents and school, so that we both, parents and teachers, are educators of our children and can help guide our children in the use of AI for their homework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In school, we will guide, we will have AI literacy, we will teach our students when to use AI and when not to use AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, that is a struggle that we all have to address as a whole of society approach; not just here in Singapore, but across the world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member's second question is about the Swedish reversal, to reverse their digital stance and to take away all these devices that they have given to the children – I believe at the age of five.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A couple of years ago, they gave it out at the age of five.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And they are reversing that, going back to analog.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some people say it is going back to analog.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have said, we continue to have physical textbooks, we continue to have didactic teaching.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have a classroom phenomenon-based learning, experiential learning, learning journeys – very teacher-centric.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And AI, as I said just now and I showed you that document, is a tool to enable learning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so for us, we are mindful that if we do not draw the distinction between general AI tools versus specifically designed learning tools, or educational AI, then it might cause us to take a wrong policy approach in Singapore and not use AI at all.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because of the changes that are happening in the world, we should make use of AI to help our students learn, because they are going to use it anyway.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Whether you supervise them or not, they will use it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is available on the Internet, in your search engines they are there.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because ultimately in higher learning and in the workplace, these tools will become ubiquitous.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so, we need to prepare our children well and not take an approach that lacks discrimination.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If it is an SLS enabled tool and is used in classroom learning, it is part of teaching and learning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is part of teachers' blended approach and I think that will enable our teachers to be able to help our children learn the cognitive aspects, the foundational knowledge more deeply.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If there are specific tools that are externally brought in where there is a parental consent element that we will then bring to the parents, then we will not allow the children to use those AI tools.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But, so far, the use of AI in general teaching, blended approaches.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is like saying, I do not want my children to have a white board, I want a black board; I want print, but I do not want an overhead projector like in the past, or PowerPoint to be used.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think we must enable our teachers to be able to perform their role and this, of course, is subject to MOE guidance and good teaching or Singapore teaching practice.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The first is, a recent The Straits Times article reported that a Primary 5 student was asked by the teacher to use ChatGPT for his homework.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And if so also, could MOE also share what is an appropriate age where students are then able to use publicly available AI tools to assist them in their learning?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My second question is, since platforms, such as Open AI and ChatGPT requires users below 18 years old to obtain parental consent, does MOE then also expect teachers to reach out to parents to get their consent to use such tools in classroom for their learning?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If so, what support will be given to teachers, because sometimes chasing parents to submit a form is significantly harder than getting the students to submit homework?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Lastly, during a recent People's Action Party Women's Union Listening Pod event, a parent asked whether parents could have the opportunity to try MOE's AI learning tools themselves, because this will help them to better experience the guardrails and also understand how to support their child in their learning.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, I would like to ask whether would MOE be open to having such engagement, to let parents try how these MOE AI learning tools?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If so, would MOE also be willing to do one in Clementi and I will be more than happy to run the parent engagement for parents living in Clementi.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On his first point, he raised an example in The Straits Times article; and we will do better to make sure that in close partnership with our educators, we apply these AI usage principles and guidelines more effectively and consistently.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because some of these general purpose tools are not appropriate for children at particular age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are terms of usage for the tool itself, not to mention our own requirements on the use of AI to scaffold learning, rather than impact it negatively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, I think the Member mentioned that some AI tools have age restrictions and if a teacher wants to use the tool in classroom, but the child is below age, we need parental consent.
Third, to let parents try out MOE's AI tools, like the Learning Feedback Assistant and so on.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I actually have a supplementary question that is related the equity paradox in AI use.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I appreciate the Minister's point about the difference between AI literacy and AI usage, and the importance of adult supervision as our children engage with AI tools from a young age.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I would like to know if the Minister could elaborate on MOE's perspective on how students from more disadvantaged backgrounds, especially those with lesser access to parental guidance or adult supervision, may end up leaning more on AI and not less, and how such dependency might actually erode the very cognitive development that it is meant to supplement, and that these children who are most at risk are precisely the ones that we need to uplift instead of having the AI use deepen the education inequality?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is an argument or that is a point that is evergreen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so, I mentioned in school how we have supervision or teacher-supervised usage of AI tools, and that applies to all the students, particularly younger ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As they leave school and go home and start using some of these tools – because SLS can only be used in the classroom when it comes to AI tools – then, the risks of them using other tools that are free-for-use on the Internet and how do we ensure that outside the classroom, there is supervision and support?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, the AI literacy that we build in all through a student's learning journey, guides them and helps to build in them that consciousness about appropriate AI usage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We hope, of course, that that is the best defence – that the child imbibes it, understands it, regardless of their socioeconomic status, they learn about it and then outside the school environment, and all through life, they are mindful of its appropriate usage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But then for the younger ones in the community and at home, partnership with parents is important, regardless of background.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we endeavour to work closely with the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so, we have homework support in different community groups, we have self-help groups that come in to provide support for children over and beyond what is available in school; and many other groups that come in to support our children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, that is a partnership we must tap on and continue to build, particularly when it comes to supporting them on appropriate AI use.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Last weekend, the People's Action Party's Women's Wing in the South West Community Development Council held a dialogue with more than 100 parents and residents on the use of AI in our children's education.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And we were glad a few Members were able to join us.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One sentiment that was surfaced echoes what the Minister has said – that before our children use AI, they need to understand what it is, its limitation as well as to have the maturity and judgement to handle it responsibly.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One of the most popular questions during that dialogue was what would be the best age for parents to talk about AI to their child.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think MDDI, the Ministry of Health (MOH) and MOE had given some recommendations and guidelines in 2025 on digital usage and use of technology at home and with children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some of that will be a useful reference for all of us as parents and as a community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But indeed, having that conversation early with your child about what AI is – because it can be embedded in your toys, online, it is available if the children have access to it at home and in the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I just came back from China last week and previously, I went to Estonia to see their AI leap in action.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in China, for instance, they start at age six, AI literacy as well as basic awareness of its growing pervasiveness throughout, like in toys and other things, so that there is literacy and understanding, and it is done in an age-appropriate way.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I think, as parents, I know it is a lot on our plate, but we want to be able to do our best for our children and guide them as they interact with all these things at home and in their toys and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, I think that is a conversation that is best started as young as possible.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wanted to follow up by asking whether the Ministry has established clear guidelines on the responsible use of AI tools by students to avoid infringement of third-party intellectual property (IP) rights.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What measures are in place to discourage the use of AI tools to generate content that imitates or reproduces the work of artists and creators without consent and attribution, and whether the Ministry will consider strengthening AI literacy programmes to place greater emphasis on ethical use, including respect for creators' rights and originality?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Certainly, at the primary school level and lower secondary, the use of AI tools are MOE-developed and used in the context of SLS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But through the MOE-developed tools, we are mindful of its safety, its quality of output, its fitness for pedagogical use and of course, in making sure that we avoid infringements of IP and other IP rights.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But ultimately, because some of the more general purpose tools, or for that matter, educational AI tools that are outside the SLS, are trained on a wider universe of knowledge and information; that the AI literacy that is taught to our children all the way till when they are young adults and all the way through the institutes of higher learning, this element of prompting, prompt engineering or usage of the tool in a way that respects IP rights that does not cause offence and that does not infringe the law.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All these are things that we need to build in as part of AI literacy all through life.
